records.addr: Southern California Gas Company proposes to Rework existing Gas Storage well Standard Sesnon 9 at Aliso Canyon UGS 0100006.
records.desc: Southern California Gas Company proposes to Rework existing Gas Storage well Standard Sesnon 9 at Aliso Canyon UGS 0100006. The intent of this project is to inspect the well integrity and remediate identified conditions as part of the Storage Integrity Management Program (SIMP). After reviewing well history, available directional surveys and inspection logs, and current wellbore configuration (casing size, restrictions, perforations, liner, etc.), a plan has been developed to return the well to service. This project includes pulling completion equipment, cleaning to total depth, performing punch and inject, and probable casing expansions as proposed and with approval from CalGEM, performing integrity tests, and running new completion tubing. Temporary equipment such as a mud pump and return bins will be utilized. No permanent facilities will be constructed during the process, and no expansion of associated facilities will be required. All waste material, including brine kill fluid, will be properly disposed of as non-hazardous or hazardous waste, as appropriate, at a facility licensed to accept the waste. The established oil field surrounding the project location consists of graded pads, wells, oilfield equipment and roadways with areas of undisturbed non-native grasses and California sage brush vegetation. The proposed project consists of the California Department of Conservation, Geologic Energy Management Division (CalGEM) approving 1 permit for Southern California Gas Company (S4700) to rework the well listed below, in the Aliso Canyon Gas Field. records.addr: Los Angeles County General Hospital Campus Master Plan
records.originalTitle: Los Angeles County General Hospital Campus Master Plan
records.desc: The Proposed Project involves implementation of the proposed Los Angeles County General Hospital Campus Master Plan. which would guide the long-term redevelopment of approximately 30.8 acres of the Project Site. including adaptive reuse of the 1.2-million-sguare-foot General Hospital Building. The Proposed Project seeks to maintain flexibility for the County to redevelop other parts of the Project Site (the approximately 51.1 acres outside of the Master Plan area) with potential County-initiated projects in the future. The Proposed Project includes the demolition of existing buildings, structures, storage containers, modular buildings, pavement, utilities, and landscaping to allow for the development of approximately 8.1 million square feet of new uses. Additionally, the Proposed Project involves seismic retrofit, selective demolition, and major improvements to facilitate adaptive reuse of the General Hospital Building and the area surrounding the building. known as the Los Angeles General Hospital-Acute Unit Historic District. The Proposed Project includes utility infrastructure improvements, circulation and transportation demand management strategies, parking, and open space and landscaping. With respect to utility infrastructure improvements, the Project Site would undergo comprehensive updates to the infrastructure network on the Project Site to meet the needs of the proposed land uses, including potable water lines, sewer lines, stormwater system, electrical lines, natural gas, and steam infrastructure. This would include decommissioning and demolition of existing outdated and inefficient energy and water distribution/collection systems, including the existing West Central Plant, consistent with assumptions in the 2014 Master Plan EIR. The Proposed Project may include development of a new centralized energy distribution system (utility plant) or a broader system of electrical and natural gas infrastructure. The Proposed Project under consideration and evaluated in the Draft SEIR represents a new proposed Master Plan that would govern redevelopment on approximately 30.8 acres of the Project Site and would largely supersede the prior Master Plan that was approved by the County. Portions of the Project Site not subject to the proposed Master Plan would continue to be governed by the previously approved 2014 Master Plan and its associated development parameters. However, because development within the remainder of the Project Site would continue pursuant to the 2014 Master Plan, the Draft SEIR evaluates potential environmental impacts associated with development across the entire Project Site to ensure that a full range of potential redevelopment on the Project Site is considered.

records.addr: Pier B On-Dock Rail Support Facility Project
records.originalTitle: Pier B On-Dock Rail Support Facility Project
records.desc: The proposed Modified Project would accommodate construction and utility installation activities for the Pier B On-Dock Rail Support Facility Project consisting of: Demolition of the Berths D52-54 Transit Shed on Pier D along Pico Avenue; Extension of an existing 36-inch diameter sewer line along West 12th Street between Harbor Avenue and Fashion Avenue; Relocation of the Control Point Foote Wye east of the Dominguez Channel to be compatible with mainline rail track configurations in the Control Point Crucero; Installation of conduit to extend an existing rail signal in the Control Point Foote Wye area; Closure of Grant Street (between Schley Avenue and Farragut Avenue) and Southern Pacific Drive (between Schley Avenue and Perry Avenue) in the City of Los Angeles; Construction of water and sewer lines on West Water Street near Interstate 710; Designation of temporary construction staging and laydown areas near the Dominguez Channel Rail Bridge, south of West Anaheim Street and west of Jackson Avenue, north and east of Carrack Avenue, and beneath the Long Beach International Gateway Bridge accessed from West Pier D Street; pavement restriping and installation of signage at the southbound I-710 Exit 1B offramp off Pico Avenue; and removal/abandonment of Sewer Main Line, north of the Toyota Logistics Services building at Pier B. Operational activities of the Pier B On-Dock Rail Support Facility Project would remain the same as discussed and analyzed in the certified EIR. Minor additions and changes to the Pier B Project consist of the following 10 areas: 1 - Berths D52-D54 Transit Shed Demolition. Demolition of the entire Transit Shed at Pier D Berths 52-54, located in the southeast portion of the project area, west of Pico Avenue, to accommodate realignment of Pico Avenue and site reconfigurations on the west side of existing Pico Avenue. The 2025 Draft SEIR proposed partial demolition of the Transit Shed, which is deemed infeasible due to cost, engineering and constructability complexities related to maintaining the remainder of the building’s integrity after partial removal of the façade and easterly portion of the Transit Shed. Thus, total demolition of the Transit Shed is now proposed. 2 - West 12th Street Sewer Line Installation. Extension of a 36-inch-diameter sewer along West 12th Street between Harbor Avenue and Fashion Avenue. 3 - Control Point Foote Wye Track Relocation and Rail Signal Extension. Relocation of the Control Point (CP) Foote Wye, east of the Dominguez Channel to be compatible with the revised mainline track configurations in the CP Crucero area. Relocation, removal, and/or protection-in-place of water, gas, storm drain, electrical, communication, and oil utilities would accommodate the relocated rail tracks. Grant Street (between approximately Schley Avenue and Farragut Avenue) and Southern Pacific Drive (between approximately Schley Avenue and Perry Avenue), within the City of Los Angeles, require closure to accommodate track realignment work. Installation of conduit to support extension of the railroad signal in the CP Foote Wye Area, west of Pennington Avenue, east of the Dominguez Channel, north of Grant Street. An existing rail signal shelter adjacent to the Dominguez Channel would be demolished. 4 - West Water Street Utility Connections. Construction of sewer and water lines on West Water Street, near the I-710 interchange at Ocean Boulevard. 5 - Dominguez Channel Rail Bridge Construction Staging and Laydown Area. Area (.03 acres) for temporary construction equipment staging and laydown for contractor activities related to the construction of the security wall under the existing and widened Dominguez Channel Rail Bridge. 6 - Pavement Restriping. Restriping and signage at the southbound I-710 Exit 1B offramp, and adjacent to Queen’s Wharf Restaurant off Pico Avenue. 7 - Anaheim Street Construction Staging and Laydown Area. Area (2.5 acres) used for temporary construction equipment staging and laydown for contractor activities related to construction, south of West Anaheim Street and west of Jackson Avenue. 8 - Carrack Avenue Construction Staging and Laydown Area. Area (12.3 acres) used for temporary construction equipment staging and laydown for contractor activities related to construction, north and east of Carrack Avenue, east of an Oil Operating Area, and south of the Toyota Logistics Services lot. 9 - Pier B Sewer Main Line Removal/Abandonment. Removal/Abandonment of a COLA-owned 27-inch sewer main line, north of the Toyota Logistics Services building at Pier B near the intersection of Pier B Street and Carrack Avenue. As part of the sewer work, POLB would take ownership of the sewer to remove/abandon it in place and would install and maintain a new manhole at the point of connection (POC) between the existing POLB/COLA sewer. Approximately 275 feet of the sewer within Southern California Edison’s (SCE) right-of-way is proposed to be removed, and approximately 2,389 ft of sewer within Toyota Logistics Services’ parking lot at Pier B is proposed to be abandoned. 10 - West Pier D Street Construction Staging and Laydown Area. Two areas (totaling 4.9 acres) for temporary construction equipment staging and laydown for contractor activities related to construction, beneath the Long Beach International Gateway Bridge, accessed from West Pier D Street.

records.addr: Amend Sections 28.06 and 28.65, Title 14, CCR Re: Recreational Gear Restrictions for White Shark (90-day Emergency Extension)
records.originalTitle: Amend Sections 28.06 and 28.65, Title 14, CCR Re: Recreational Gear Restrictions for White Shark (90-day Emergency Extension)
records.desc: The proposed project would extend the emergency amendments to Title 14, California Code of Regulations (CCR), sections 28.06 and 28.65 regarding finfish fishing gear restrictions and the take of white sharks. The proposed extension would continue the requirement to immediately release hooked white sharks and prohibit removing white sharks from the water. The proposed extension would also continue the also prohibit the use of wire or metallic lines or leaders or hooks greater than one and one-half inches in maximum inside diameter when fishing from the shoreline (including beaches, banks, piers, jetties, breakwaters, docks, and other man-made structures connected to the shore) or within 1,000 yards of the mean high tide line in ocean waters south of Pigeon Point (San Mateo County, 37° 11' N. lat.). This project extends the emergency rule originally adopted at the June 17-18, 2026 Fish and Game Commission meeting (Office of Administrative Law File Number 2026-0626-01E). The El Nino conditions that prompted the emergency are continuing and anticipated to increase through the fall, necessitating an extension of the emergency regulations. The extension of the emergency amendments are necessary to further protect white sharks from illegal fishing activities and to help prevent incidents between hooked white sharks and ocean users in the same vicinity. White sharks are an important apex predator in the marine ecosystem and are protected under state and federal fishing regulations. There have been several incidents involving pier and beach anglers either intentionally targeting white sharks or accidentally hooking them with very heavy fishing gear; the incidents have resulted in the death of at least three white sharks this year. Additionally, in 2014, a swimmer was bitten by a white shark that had been hooked by a pier angler. This year, a forecasted strong El Niño oceanic event is anticipated to increase the presence of white sharks in California coastal waters, which will increase their availability to anglers and the potential for human interactions with hooked sharks. Young white sharks are already being observed in significantly higher numbers in southern California. Because of this, an emergency situation exists that requires an immediate need to curtail illegal targeted fishing for white sharks, help ensure accidentally hooked sharks are released alive, and help prevent another incident where a hooked shark bites an ocean user or the heavy gear used to catch such sharks entangles a person in the water.
records.lastNote: The proposed project would extend the emergency amendments to Title 14, California Code of Regulations (CCR), sections 28.06 and 28.65 regarding finfish fishing gear restrictions and the take of white sharks. The proposed extension would continue the requirement to immediately release hooked white sharks and prohibit removing white sharks from the water.

records.addr: 2028 Amendments to the California Green Building Standards Code Pursuant to Senate Bill 745
records.originalTitle: 2028 Amendments to the California Green Building Standards Code Pursuant to Senate Bill 745
records.desc: In response to the Drought-Resistant Buildings Act (SB 745), the Building Standards Commission (BSC) is proposing amendments to CALGreen, Part 11 of Title 24.The proposed amendments are intended to reduce potable water use in new nonresidential buildings by elevating certain existing voluntary water-efficiency measures to mandatory requirements. The proposed requirements would provide multiple compliance options to accommodate varying building types and regional conditions throughout California. If adopted, the amendments would be incorporated into the 2028 CALGreen, scheduled for publication on July 1, 2028, and would take effect on January 1, 2029.The Project consists of changes to building design and construction requirements that would apply statewide. Accordingly, the geographic scope of the Project encompasses the entire State of California. Although CALGreen establishes requirements applicable to new construction, the Project does not propose, authorize, or induce the construction of any new buildings or development. Rather, CALGreen regulates how applicable buildings and improvements are designed and constructed when such construction occurs; it does not determine where or when new construction takes place.

records.addr: Former Crocker Plating Works Facility – West Lot Removal Action Workplan for Soil
records.originalTitle: Former Crocker Plating Works Facility – West Lot Removal Action Workplan for Soil
records.desc: The project consists of the excavation and off-site disposal of soils that have been impacted by total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPH) characterized as oil range organics (ORO), hexavalent chromium (Cr6+), and lead at the Former Crocker Plating Works Facility - West Lot property located at 5879 and 5887 Crocker Street in Los Angeles California (Site). The Site encompasses an area of approximately 0.24 acres. The estimated volume of soil proposed for removal, minus any additional soil removed for excavation sloping (sidewall stability) purposes, will be approximately 370 bank cubic yards (bcy). The project is estimated to take approximately 3 months. Background: The Site consists of two City-owned parcels identified by the Los Angeles County Assessor’s Office by Assessor Identification Numbers 6006-029-900 (5879 Crocker Street) and 6006-029-901 (5887 Crocker Street). The Site is currently vacant but was previously used as a parking lot with outdoor storage in connection with the former Crocker Plating Works business that operated immediately east of the Site at 5888 and 5910 Crocker Street. The Site and surrounding parcels are zoned “RD - Restricted Density Multiple Dwelling Zone”. The Site is located within a mixed residential, commercial, and manufacturing area of south-central Los Angeles, with a long history of offsite businesses and industries (both historical and active) that include uses such as metal plating, furniture manufacturing and motor vehicle repair. The City of Los Angeles plans to redevelop the Site for high density residential housing. Previous Investigations: Multiple Phase I and Phase II Environmental Site Assessments (ESAs) have been conducted at the Site under the oversight of the Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC); these ESAs have involved the assessment of Site soil, groundwater, and soil vapor. Soil at the Site has been analyzed for various analytical suites including petroleum hydrocarbons, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs), Cr6+, Title 22 metals polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), organochlorine pesticides (OCPs), and cyanide. Assessed Site soils appear to be sporadically impacted by ORO, arsenic (one sample location at a depth of 90 feet below ground surface), Cr6+, and lead at concentrations exceeding screening levels for a residential land use scenario. Results indicate that shallow Site soil impacts warrant remediation, while identified groundwater and soil vapor impacts either do not represent a complete or potentially complete exposure pathway, or can be adequately mitigated through the implementation of engineering controls emplaced during Site redevelopment. Accordingly, the RAW is intended to solely address impacts to Site soil via soil excavation in preparation for subsequent Site redevelopment activities. Project Activities: The proposed soil remedy project activities include the following: • Excavation at five 20-foot by 20-foot areas (totaling approximately 370 bcy) located across the Site to a maximum total depth of approximately 8 feet below ground surface (bgs) to remove ORO, Cr6+, and lead-impacted soil. Off-site disposal will require approximately 25-30 truck trips to one or more of the following facilities: California, Simi Valley Regional Landfill in eastern Ventura County, California, La Paz Landfill in southwest Arizona, South Yuma Landfill in southwest Arizona, Kettleman Hills Landfill in Kings County, California. • The evaluation of underlying and sidewall soils for visual or olfactory indications of previously unidentified impacts. • Post-excavation confirmation soil sampling activities. • Preparation of a Soil Management Plan (SMP) to ensure that any residual impacted soil (if encountered) will be managed in accordance with pre-established processes and procedures that will be protective of human health and the environment. Because geotechnical assessments conducted at the Site in preparation for Site redevelopment have resulted in the conclusion that the uppermost five feet of Site soil beneath proposed building footprints will need to be removed and replaced prior to construction, the RAW proposes leaving the completed excavations open, with all excavation sidewalls sloped to mitigate the potential for fall-related injuries to Site visitors or trespassers, and to preclude stormwater runoff from the excavated areas. The Site will be left in compliance with stormwater best management practices (BMPs) adopted to prevent soil runoff post-RAW implementation. A grading permit and clearances will be required from the City of Los Angeles. The project is also subject to: • South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD) Rule 1166 – Volatile Organic Compound Emissions from Decontamination of Soil - which requires owners or operators excavating, grading, handling, or treating VOC-contaminated soil to implement an approved VOC mitigation plan and provide notification to control emissions during decontamination activities • SCAQMD Rule 1466 – Control of Particulate Emissions from Soils with Toxic Air Contaminants. Mandates that any earth-moving activity disturbing soil contaminated with specified toxic air contaminants at designated cleanup sites must employ dust-control measures, implement PM10 monitoring, and adhere to notification, signage, and recordkeeping requirements to minimize off-site particulate emissions. • SCAQMD Rule 403 – Dust Control, to minimize emission of fugitive dust. Monitoring will be conducted during all soil disturbance activities by qualified technicians under the supervision of a Certified Industrial Hygienist. The following additional permits may be required: • California Department of Public Health Abatement of Lead Hazards Evaluation Notification Form 8551 and Lead Hazard Evaluation Report Form 8552 or latest versions. • Los Angeles Departments of Transportation and Bureau of Engineering: Traffic control and encroachment permits for work activities that require encroachment and/or traffic control or pedestrian control measures, and implementation of the transportation plan. • Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Board: Stormwater Pollution and Prevention Plan. • Los Angeles Department of Building and Safety (LADBS) and Los Angeles Department of Water and Power: Temporary water connection (fire hydrant) installation and meter permits, if necessary. In addition, planning documents have been prepared for the following: Health and Safety, Soil Management, Remedial Design Implementation, Community Air Monitoring, and Traffic and Transportation. Although not anticipated, in the event biological, cultural or historical resources are discovered in the course of project activities, work will be suspended while a qualified biologist, cultural or historical specialist makes an assessment of the area and arrangements are made to protect or preserve any resources that are discovered. If human remains are discovered, no further disturbance will occur in the location where the remains are found, and the County Coroner will be notified pursuant to the Health and Safety Code, Chapter 2, Section 7050.5.

records.desc: The Proposed Project involves the adoption of a new ordinance known as the “Landscape and Site Design Ordinance” (Proposed Ordinance) that will amend the City's current Landscape Ordinance (No. 170,978), Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC) Sections 12.40 through 12.43, previously adopted in May 1996 and amended in April 2005. The proposed amendment to LAMC Sections 12.40 through 12.43 will create new landscape and site design objective standards (Landscape and Site Design Point System) using a dynamic and flexible performance-based point system, in order to implement healthy building design and climate-adapted site design. Through established point targets dependent on project types, the Point System will establish a more efficient and effective implementation process. The objective design standards represent a more comprehensive approach to site design that aligns with broader Citywide policy goals of climate resilience, designing for health and the protection and enhancement of the City’s urban forest and biodiversity. Related amendments to LAMC Sections 12.03, 12.10.5, 12.11.5, 12.12.2, 12.13, 12.21, 12.21.1, 12.40, 12.41, 12.42, 12.43, 13.08, 13.09, 14.00, 19.04, 62.177 and 91.7012 are necessary in order to effectuate the Landscape and Site Design Ordinance and Point System. The proposed Landscape and Site Design Ordinance will apply Citywide and will address pressing sustainability and health-related needs, building upon The Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles, the General Plan’s Health and Wellness Element, and the Citywide Design Guidelines that are in effect today. Policy 2.2 of The Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles (Chapter 2.2) addresses healthy building design and construction and the relationship of health to the built environment. This policy encourages the design and rehabilitation of buildings and sites for healthy living and working conditions, promoting enhanced pedestrian-oriented circulation, lighting, attractive and open stairs, healthy building materials and universal accessibility. Secondly, a future Implementation Program identified in the Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles (Program 36) speaks to streamlining and updating the 1996 City of Los Angeles Landscape Guidelines and Ordinance to better respond to climate change and healthy communities. The proposed Landscape and Site Design Point System implements Policy 2.2 of the Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles through a set of objective standards that are organized into the following three design approaches: (1) Pedestrian-First Design, (2) 360 Degree Design and (3) Climate Adapted Landscape and Site Design, similar to the Citywide Design Guidelines. Under each design approach, the standards are further organized under topical categories accompanied by corresponding strategies that are identified as either Mandatory or Elective, each with an assigned point value. The Ordinance will apply to residential and non-residential projects that may employ any of the standards in each category to obtain a required total of points, some of which will be mandatory, with a minimum of three points in each category and at least eight Designing for Health standards. To encourage the protection and expansion of tree canopy and heat island reduction in climate-vulnerable communities, projects that are in a mapped “Health and Urban Forest Equity Priority” area, per the draft Zoning Information file that accompanies the Proposed Ordinance, will be required to meet two additional health-related standards in the Landscape and Site Design Point System. These projects will also be eligible for up to five additional bonus points if certain standards related to tree canopy conservation, tree planting, and reduction of climate impacts are selected. Industrial or hybrid-Industrial projects and surface parking lot projects must meet a total of 15 points, through a combination of Mandatory and Elective standards. The proposed Landscape and Site Design Ordinance also includes a new definition for Outdoor Amenity Areas to support the integration of indoor and outdoor spaces. Outdoor Amenity Areas are outdoor spaces that are covered with overhead structures like patios, terraces, and courtyards and/or outdoor spaces that are only partially enclosed. This new definition and set of standards, allows for creative design solutions for outdoor areas that provide shade and comfort without counting these outdoor spaces toward the building’s floor area and height.
records.lastNote: The Proposed Project involves the adoption of a new ordinance known as the “Landscape and Site Design Ordinance” (Proposed Ordinance) that will amend the City's current Landscape Ordinance (No. 170,978), Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC) Sections 12.40 through 12.43, previously adopted in May 1996 and amended in April 2005.

records.desc: BOE-79 (Project) is a later activity undertaken pursuant to the Sidewalk Repair Program (SRP) as a project eligible for credit under the Willits Settlement (Mark Willits, et al. v. City of Los Angeles [United States District Court Case No. CV10-05782 CBM (RZX)]) and subject to Los Angeles Municipal Code 62.104.1. The Project encompasses sidewalk reconstruction, cross-slope adjustments, curb and gutter repairs, and installation of accessible curb ramps across 160 addresses CD 8. Based on site-specific arborists evaluations, severe tree root uplift has disrupted sidewalk across the project locations. Alternative tree retention options (such as root pruning or sidewalk ramping) were determined infeasible because root pruning would compromise structural tree stability and public safety. Consequently, the Project includes Board of Public Works (BPW) approval for the removal of six street trees (2 Jacarandas, 3 Camphor, 1 Chinese Elm). BOE-79 mandates compliance with the SRP Street Tree Policy and Mandatory Project Design Features Policy.

records.desc: The site is part of the Camino Nuevo Charter Academy, Burlington Campus, comprising of eleven (11) lots within the C2-2, R4-2, and C4-2 Zones. The campus is developed with an elementary school, school yard, parking lot, single-family residence, pre-school, and middle school. The single-family residence located on Lot 16 is not operating as a school, however; the project requests a rear yard setback adjustment on Lot 16 to connect the school yard and elementary school to the pre-school and middle school via a pedestrian walkway. The campus has approximately 482.92 feet of street frontage along Burlington Avenue to the east and 150.09 feet of frontage along Wilshire Boulevard to the north. The project site is limited to four R4 zoned lots on a rectangular-shaped parcel of land covering approximately 30,750 square-feet of net lot area. The subject site is improved with a school yard, parking lot, and single-family residence. The project site has approximately 205 feet of street frontage along Burlington Avenue to the east. The project consists of the construction of new fences, walls, and a covered pedestrian walkway. The applicant is requesting a Director’s Adjustment to allow the construction, use, and maintenance of a 10-foot-wide covered pedestrian walkway with a maximum height of 13 feet and 8 inches in the rear yard setback, and eleven (11) over-in-height fences/walls with a maximum height of 10 to 13 feet within the front, side, and rear yard setbacks. The project does not propose demolition of existing buildings or tree removal. All buildings and trees will remain. Since the project is for the construction of new fences, walls, a covered pedestrian walkway and no physical changes to the existing buildings are proposed, this project qualifies for the Class 3 (New Construction or Conversion of Small Structures) Categorical Exemption.

records.addr: Lincoln Park Neighborhood Green Street Network
records.originalTitle: Lincoln Park Neighborhood Green Street Network
records.desc: The Project includes three components: Lincoln Park Lake Improvements; installation of approximately 37 to 50 drywells with associated storm drain infrastructure; and installation of approximately 172 street trees along selected public streets in Lincoln Heights. Lake improvements would include sediment removal, shoreline stabilization, pump house and circulation and aeration system upgrades, passive bioswales, and associated landscape and hardscape modifications. The drywells would capture, treat, and infiltrate runoff from an approximately 125-acre drainage area and would be sized to achieve an 80 percent long-term pollutant load reduction. The Project would provide short-term water quality improvement in Lincoln Park Lake, reduce pollutant loads to the Los Angeles River, enhance lake, park, and streetscape infrastructure, reduce localized flooding, increase groundwater recharge, and improve the neighborhood’s visual quality through landscaping. These objectives would support the Safe Clean Water Program and broader water quality goals for the Upper Los Angeles River watershed.
records.lastNote: The Project includes three components: Lincoln Park Lake Improvements; installation of approximately 37 to 50 drywells with associated storm drain infrastructure; and installation of approximately 172 street trees along selected public streets in Lincoln Heights.

records.desc: The Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP) plans to remove a series of artistic panels currently installed on the exterior surface of an existing water tank in the southern portion of the Scattergood Generating Station located at 12700 Vista Del Mar, Los Angeles, CA 90293. Since its installation in 2018, the panels have experienced sun-related deterioration, including fading and material degradation. In 2023, LADWP initiated efforts to repair and replace affected panels. LADWP will remove all artistic panels from the water tank. Following removal of the panels, LADWP will conduct surface restoration activities to preserve the structural integrity and appearance of the water tank. Restoration activities may include rust removal, surface cleaning, spot repairs, application of protective coatings, paint, and/or new panel installations. The activities are limited to maintenance, repair, and minor alteration of an existing facility and will not involve ground disturbance, expansion of use, or any changes to facility operations.

records.desc: The Proposed Project is an update of the following three Community Plans: (1) Canoga Park-Winnetka-Woodland Hills-West Hills Community Plan; (2) Encino-Tarzana Community Plan; and (3) Reseda-West Van Nuys Community Plan. records.addr: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, Honeywell Aerospace US, LLC. (Honeywell), Torrance, California
records.originalTitle: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, Honeywell Aerospace US, LLC. (Honeywell), Torrance, California
records.desc: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20, Sec. 66270.61, has issued an Emergency Permit to Honeywell, (EPA ID# CAD071896336) to treat hazardous waste through a controlled reaction with chemical solutions. Specifically, one (1) 100-gram container of Picric Acid must be stabilized prior to transport to an authorized hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facility. This chemical is currently being stored at Honeywell located at 2525 West 190th Street Torrance, California 90504. DTSC has determined as a safety precaution to prevent an accident or severe injury, an Emergency Permit should be issued to chemically stabilize the hazardous waste prior to storage and eventual transportation off-site by Clean Harbors Environmental Services (Clean Harbors). Background: Shock and/or temperature sensitive materials can decompose or detonate with external energy when dry or concentrated. If the material is improperly handled, there is a potential for a reaction, which includes fire, deflagration, or detonation. Due to the presence of shock-sensitive materials, DTSC considers these chemicals to be an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment. Chemical stabilization is recommended prior to transport to a permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facility. Project Activities: The treatment of this hazardous waste involves the addition of solutions to the containers in a controlled manner to reduce the reactive or ignitable characteristics of the chemicals. Treatment will take place within a designated exclusion zone. Only technicians from Clean Harbors will be allowed in the exclusion zone. Movement, preparation, and treatment of the containers will be in accordance with established standards. Within 10 business days of the expiration of this permit, Honeywell will submit a final report, signed in accordance with Title 22, CCR Sec. 66270.11(d). The report shall include certification that the treatment area has been cleared of all residual hazardous waste generated from this emergency treatment and all generated waste has been properly managed. The Emergency Permit is effective beginning October 6, 2026 and shall expire on December 6, 2026.

records.originalTitle: UCLA Research Park East Core and Shell Improvements
records.desc: The proposed UCLA Research Park East Core and Shell Improvements (Core and Shell) Project is the first in a series of phased projects at UCLA Research Park. UCLA Research Park consists of two connected buildings totaling approximately 1,308,000 gross square feet (gsf) on 9.2 acres. The Core and Shell Project would retrofit the East building (10800 West Pico Boulevard), a 706,000-gsf, three-story facility with two underground levels, for multi-tenant use, including biomedical research and quantum physics laboratories, which would be developed in subsequent tenant improvement projects. An Advanced Work Phase of the Core and Shell Project would involve interior and roof demolition, site and utilities preparation, and procurement of long lead-time equipment. In accordance with CEQA, an Initial Study/Mitigated Negative Declaration (IS/MND) (State Clearinghouse No. 2026050140) has been prepared for full buildout of the UCLA Research Park project, including future phases.

records.desc: Dockweiler SB is host to a federally endangered California least tern colony. In the mid 1980’s, a portion of the beach northwest of Ballona Creek was enclosed to prevent human activity and ground based predators from disturbing the colony. In 2006 the enclosed area was expanded to its current footprint and a new fence was installed. The fencing material is in an advanced state of deterioration. Gaps in the mesh and collapse of arm wires has allowed humans and predators to easily access the colony, and related disturbance is associate with colony abandonment in 2022. Grant funding for Angeles District to replace the existing fence was obtained in 2023. A contractor will replace ~2,500 linear feet of chain link fencing protecting the ~7.5 acre California least tern colony, using heavy equipment and augering new post holes to a depth of ~4’.

There will be six (6) parking spaces with no guest parking spaces within the dedicated parking garage located at ground level. The proposed project also includes four (4) bicycle parking spaces, and 1,013.8 square feet of usable open space. Also, the proposed project is includes a cut and export of approximately 66.7 cubic yards, and an overexcavation/recompaction 468 cubic yards. The number of units and size is not unusual for the vicinity of the subject site and is similar in scope to other existing multi-family dwellings in the area. Thus, there are no unusual circumstances which may lead to a significant effect on the environment.

records.addr: Cost Share Agreement Between City of Long Beach and City of Los Angeles for Environmental Services at Long Beach Leads Extension Parcels LBX/MY-851 and LBX/SE-8
records.originalTitle: Cost Share Agreement Between City of Long Beach and City of Los Angeles for Environmental Services at Long Beach Leads Extension Parcels LBX/MY-851 and LBX/SE-8
records.desc: The proposed action approves a cost share agreement with the City of Los Angeles for environmental services at Long Beach Leads Extension Parcels LBX/MY-851 and LBX/SE-853, including historical and future costs in an amount not to exceed $1,100,000, with a term commencing on the date of agreement signature through October 31, 2030. The Cities of Long Beach and Los Angeles have jointly owned LBX/MY-851 and LBX/SE-853 since 1994 and 2020, respectively. Both parcels are under regulatory oversight by the Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Board, which requires groundwater monitoring, free product recovery, and remediation of soil and groundwater. The Port of Los Angeles (POLA) has managed the environmental regulatory responsibilities since 2007. The agreement allows the Port of Long Beach (POLB) to reimburse the POLA for previous testing, monitoring, reporting, and remediation actions, and establishes a cost share arrangement between POLB and POLA for environmental work to be performed through October 31, 2030.

records.desc: The project is for the change of use from a 937 square-foot business/residence to a 1,988 square-foot preschool, the demolition of 663 square feet of the existing building, and the construction of a two (2)-story addition, for a total building floor area of 1,988 square feet, with four (4) vehicle parking spaces. The project requires five (5) cubic yards of fill. The project site does not contain any Protected Trees or Shrubs. There is one (1) tree in the adjacent public right-of-way that will be maintained. The building will have a maximum building height of 29 feet and two (2) inches. The project requires the following: 1. Pursuant to LAMC Chapter 1, Section 13.08 and the Cypress Park and Glassell Park Community Design Overlay (CDO), a CDO Director’s Determination for the change of use from a 937 square-foot business/residence to a 1,988 square-foot preschool, the demolition of 663 square feet of the existing building, and the construction of a two (2)-story addition, for a total building floor area of 1,988 square feet. The project is located within the Northeast Los Angeles Community Plan which designates the project site for Neighborhood Commercial land uses with corresponding zones of C1, C1.5, C2, C4, and RAS3. The project site is zoned [Q]C1.5-1VL-CDO. The project is consistent with the applicable general plan land use designation and all applicable general plan policies as well as with the applicable zoning designation and regulations. The project site is wholly within the City of Los Angeles, on a site that is approximately 0.12 acres in size. Lots adjacent to the project site are developed with the following urban uses: commercial, single-family, and multi-family developments. The site is currently developed with a business/residence and the new use will be a preschool. The site is surrounded by development and therefore is not, and has no value as, a habitat for endangered, rare or threatened species. In addition, there are zero (0) Protected Trees on-site. The project will be subject to Regulatory Compliance Measures (RCMs), which require compliance with the City of Los Angeles Noise Ordinance, pollutant discharge, dewatering, stormwater mitigations; and Best Management Practices for stormwater runoff. These RCMs will ensure the project will not have significant impacts on noise and water. Furthermore, the project does not exceed the threshold criteria established by LADOT for preparing a transportation study. Interim thresholds were developed by DCP staff based on CalEEMod model runs relying on reasonable assumptions, consulting with AQMD staff, and surveying published air quality studies for which criteria air pollutants did not exceed the established SCAQMD construction and operational thresholds. The project site will be adequately served by all public utilities and services given that the change of use from a one (1)-story business/residence to a two (2)-story preschool totaling 1,988 square feet, with four (4) automobile parking spaces, will be on a site that has been previously developed and is consistent with the General Plan. Therefore, the project meets all of the Criteria for the Class 32.

records.desc: The Applicant proposes a Tentative Tract Map to merge two (2) existing lots into one (1) ground lot resulting in total lot area of approximately 13,761 square-feet, for the purpose of 30 new condominiums in a proposed multi-family residential building. On October 17, 2024, the Department of City Planning issued a Class 32 Categorical Exemption (ENV-20205018-CE) to permit the demolition of two (2) existing single-family dwellings and two (2) detached garages, and the construction, use and maintenance of a five (5)-story multifamily residential building containing 30 dwelling units, including three (3) units restricted to Extremely Low Income Households, in conjunction with an approval for the Transit Oriented Communities Affordable Housing Incentive Program (Case No. DIR-2020-5017-TOC-HCA). The project site is located at 1537-1541 South Hayworth Avenue within the Wilshire Community Plan. The proposed project is 57 feet in height and comprises 38,499 square feet of floor area. Demolition permits for the existing improvements were issued on August 27, 2024; however, at the time of writing, demolition had not yet begun. A building permit for the multi-family building was issued on March 5, 2026; however, at the time of writing, construction had not yet begun. The project proposes the cut and export of 9,682 (12,064 with a 25-percent swell factor) cubic yards of soil and the fill of 31 cubic yards. No import of soil is proposed. The project proposes the removal of eleven (11) existing on-site trees and the planting of ten (10) trees, consisting of 10 ground floor on-site trees. The three (3) Street Trees adjacent to the site were originally proposed for preservation subject to the discretion of the Urban Forestry Division. However, for purposes of conservative analysis and the requirements of CEQA, Planning has analyzed the worst-case potential for removal of all street trees. At the time of writing, the Urban Forestry Division has approved the removal of one (1) of the three (3) Street Trees. This environmental analysis does not authorize the removal of any street trees without prior approval of Urban Forestry, in compliance with LAMC Sections 62.169 and 62.170 and their applicable findings. Note, no Street Tree or protected tree may be removed without prior approval of the Board of Public Works/Urban Forestry (BPW) under LAMC Sections 62.161 - 62.171.
records.lastNote: The Applicant proposes a Tentative Tract Map to merge two (2) existing lots into one (1) ground lot resulting in total lot area of approximately 13,761 square-feet, for the purpose of 30 new condominiums in a proposed multi-family residential building.

records.addr: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, City of Los Angeles, Department of General Services, Los Angeles, California
records.originalTitle: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, City of Los Angeles, Department of General Services, Los Angeles, California
records.desc: Project Description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20, Sec. 66270.61, has issued an Emergency Permit to City of Los Angeles, Department of General Services (EPA ID# CAD981576077) to treat hazardous waste through a controlled reaction with a chemical solution. Specifically, two (2) 1-liter containers of Diethyl Ether must be stabilized prior to transport to an authorized hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facility. This chemical is currently being stored at the City of Los Angeles, Department of General Services located at 2319 Dorris Place, Los Angeles, California 90031. DTSC has determined as a safety precaution to prevent an accident or severe injury, an Emergency Permit should be issued to chemically stabilize the hazardous waste prior to storage and eventual transportation off-site. Background: The containers have peroxide formation present on either the inside, outside, or the bottom of the chemical’s containers, as well as the thread container caps. The presence of peroxide formation may be unstable at relatively low concentrations, resulting in fire and/or explosion if improperly handled. Due to the presence of peroxide formation, DTSC considers this chemical to be an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment. Chemical stabilization is recommended prior to transport to a permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facility. Project Activities: The treatment of these hazardous wastes involves the addition of a solution to the containers in a controlled manner to reduce the reactive or ignitable characteristics of the chemical. Treatment will take place within a designated exclusion zone. Only technicians from Clean Harbors will be allowed in the exclusion zone. Movement, preparation, and treatment of the containers will be in accordance with established standards. Within 10 business days of the expiration of this permit, the City of Los Angeles, Department of General Services will submit a final report, signed in accordance with Title 22, CCR Sec. 66270.11(d). The report shall include certification that the treatment area has been cleared of all residual hazardous waste generated from this emergency treatment and all generated waste has been properly managed. The Emergency Permit is effective beginning August 19, 2026 and shall expire on October 19, 2026.

records.addr: Vineland Family Housing Removal Action Workplan
records.originalTitle: Vineland Family Housing Removal Action Workplan
records.desc: The project consists of implementing a Removal Action Workplan (RAW) to address concentrations of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in soil and sub-slab vapor on a 2.18 acre parcel located at 8015 and 8025 Vineland Avenue in Los Angeles, California (“Site”). The RAW proposes implementation of a vapor intrusion mitigation system (VIMS) with passive sub-slab ventilation (SSV) beneath two buildings that are proposed for development at the Site, along with adoption of a Land Use Covenant (LUC). Background: The Site is located in the Sun Valley neighborhood of Los Angeles and is identified as Los Angeles County Assessor’s Parcel Number (APN) 2314-006-002. The Site is an “L-shaped” parcel, roughly bounded on the west and northwest by apartments and residential properties, on the south by Strathern Street, on the east by Vineland Avenue, and on the north and southeast by commercial properties. The Site is currently vacant except for the concrete building foundation of a former 20,181-square-foot building, historically used as a grocery/market, which was destroyed in a fire in July 2021. Additionally, a temporary building and storage containers associated with a recycling center are located off Strathern Street in the southwest portion of the Site. The remaining portions of the Site consist of asphalt-paved parking areas and driveways providing access from Strathern Street to the south and Vineland Avenue to the east. DTSC and Las Palmas Housing and Development Corporation entered into a Voluntary Cleanup Agreement (Docket Number HSA-FY21/22-115 signed on March 29, 2022) to address contaminants on the Site. The Site is planned to be redeveloped with mixed-used commercial and multi-family/senior residential uses. Redevelopment of the Site entails the construction of a 6-story mixed-use building on the eastern/central portion of the Site (Vineland Apartments), which would include 136 affordable apartment dwelling units, 26,056 square feet of ground-floor commercial space, and underground parking. Additional development on the western portion (Strathern Senior Apartments) includes a 5-story building consisting of 97 affordable senior housing units, common areas, and underground parking. Two single-story underground parking structures are proposed to a depth of 12 feet beneath the majority of the Site apart from the southern portion of the senior development. Vehicular access to the Site is proposed at Vineland Avenue via two separate driveways and Strathern Street via one driveway, with reciprocal access at the northern adjacent property. It is noted that the City of Los Angeles previously determined that each of the land use development projects with which the subject RAW is associated are statutorily exempt from CEQA as a ministerial action pursuant to Public Resources Code Section 21080(b)(1) and Los Angeles Municipal Code (“LAMC”) Section 12.22 A.31. The City issued SB 35 Letters of Compliance dated April 20, 2023, to the RP regarding the ministerial approvals. The subject site mitigation and cleanup activities set forth in the RAW are considered discretionary approvals subject to CEQA and are outside the scope of the activities determined to be statutorily exempt. Previous Investigations: Investigations at the Site indicate that the primary Chemicals of Potential Concern (COPCs) include PCE, benzene, ethylbenzene, chloroform, dichlorodifluoromethane, and 1,2-DCA, which were detected at concentrations exceeding applicable screening levels (SLs). Per information provided in the RAW, soil investigation results did not indicate any COPCs in soil exceeding SLs, or potential on-Site sources of the reported soil vapor impacts. Groundwater is estimated to be at a depth of greater than 300 feet below ground surface (bgs). Based on the soil sampling results, soil and/or groundwater does not appear to have been potentially impacted by historical operations at the Site. Project Activities: The activities outlined in the RAW consist of implementing a VIMS with passive SSV beneath the two proposed buildings. The SSV system is designed for soil vapor to be passively diverted into the venting system and safely discharged to the atmosphere by means of vertical vent risers terminating at the building roof line. The venting system will consist of a sub-slab gravel layer beneath the entire footprint of the building that contains low-profile, 1-inch sub-slab collection pipes, which will transition to 3-inch rigid polyvinyl chloride pipe where penetration though building footers occurs. The collection pipes will be connected to carbon steel vertical risers along the building exterior that terminate above the roof line. An impervious membrane barrier will be installed above the sub-slab passive venting system and beneath the entire extent of the building footprint. The horizontal membrane barrier will consist of a minimum cured thickness of 60 mil (0.06 inches) Liquid Boot Plus VI-20 geomembrane. Monitoring probes will be placed within the gravel layer (below the membrane) and terminate in monitoring vaults outside the building perimeter wall. Sub-slab soil vapor monitoring probes will be used to monitor soil vapor concentrations under the slab. The VIMS installation will be implemented as part of the same construction activities which have already been approved for development through the City of Los Angeles’s SB 35 streamlined environmental review process. Installation of the VIMS would not require any substantial changes to the timing or duration of site preparation and construction activities, the type of equipment utilized as part of site preparation and construction, or the number of workers involved or number of worker transportation trips for the site preparation and construction processes. VIMS installation will not require any changes to the site boundaries, building footprint, aesthetic design, or operational characteristics from what was previously evaluated. In addition, a Land Use Covenant (LUC) will be recorded with Los Angeles County to ensure notifications are made to DTSC prior to any future earthwork activities at the Site, prevent disturbance of the vapor barrier, and ensure the prohibition of any groundwater extraction. Although not anticipated, in the event biological, cultural or historical resources are discovered in the course of project activities, work will be suspended while a qualified biologist, cultural or historical specialist makes an assessment of the area and arrangements are made to protect or preserve any resources that are discovered. If human remains are discovered, no further disturbance will occur in the location where the remains are found, and the County Coroner will be notified pursuant to the Health and Safety Code, Chapter 2, Section 7050.5.

The new ordinance (LAMC 62.104.1) revises the way sidewalk repairs pursuant to the Willits Settlement, are reviewed and approved, and is intended generally to improve and streamline the implementation process. The primary components of the ordinance include: • Specific parameters to enable most sidewalk repairs to proceed as ministerial approvals, not subject to further environmental review applicable to discretionary actions. • A streamlined discretionary approval process for sidewalk repair projects falling ou1side the specific parameters allowed for a ministerial sidewalk repair approval. • A streamlined discretionary approval process for sidewalk repair projects involving the proposed removal of three or more street trees. • A revised Street Tree Retention, Removal and Replacement Policy. • Mandatory Project Design Features (PDFs) generally consisting of regulatory compliance measures and standard construction conditions and procedures.

records.addr: Scattergood Generating Station Units 1 and 2 Green Hydrogen-Ready Modernization Project
records.originalTitle: Scattergood Generating Station Units 1 and 2 Green Hydrogen-Ready Modernization Project
records.desc: The Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP) proposes to construct and operate a rapid-response combined-cycle generation system (CCGS) at Scattergood Generating Station. The Proposed Project would replace the generation capacity of existing Scattergood Units 1 and 2, which are conventional natural-gas-fired steam-boiler generators that would be removed from service, with a CCGS capable of operating on a fuel mixture of natural gas and a minimum of 30 percent hydrogen by volume. The proposed CCGS would consist of a combustion-turbine generator and a steam-turbine generator operating in tandem. Additional facilities or ancillary functions required to support the proposed CCGS include, but are not limited to, an air-cooled condenser, wet-surface air cooler, gas compressors, switchyard upgrades, and a dedicated pipeline for industrial wastewater discharge. With the implementation of expanded renewable generation resources, improvements to transmission systems, increased energy storage, and other elements of the LADWP carbon-free energy system outlined in the SLTRP, LADWP’s in-basin generation units, including the Proposed Project, are anticipated to be utilized less frequently than under current conditions, primarily to meet peaks in the requirement for electrical power during high demand days that exceed renewable energy production and energy storage capacity. In addition, the CCGS would be used during relatively short-term periods when the renewable generation sources and/or transmission assets become unavailable due to emergency circumstances. Therefore, although anticipated to be operated less frequently, this firm local generation capability is crucial to maintaining the resilience and reliability of the LADWP power system. The necessary infrastructure for the production, delivery, and storage of green hydrogen needed to support the Proposed Project currently does not exist. While it is anticipated that a sufficient market supply of green hydrogen may be available to support the Proposed Project dual-fuel CCGS when it is fully commissioned by the end of 2029, the details of the green hydrogen system are currently unknown. Therefore, this DEIR does not address the supply of green hydrogen to Scattergood Generating Station, which will be analyzed in a separate environmental review and approval process when the necessary information to support an adequate analysis of potential impacts is available. LADWP would not implement or operate this hydrogen infrastructure but would be a purchaser of hydrogen to supply the Proposed Project. Nonetheless, because the combustion-turbine generator component of the proposed CCGS would be capable of operating on a mixture of natural gas and hydrogen fuel, the impacts related to the combustion of such a fuel mixture are analyzed in this DEIR. Construction of the Proposed Project is anticipated to begin in 2026 and the CCGS would be fully operational by the end of 2029.

records.desc: The proposed project includes the rehabilitation, expansion, and construction, use, and maintenance of historic church-related facilities measuring approximately 16,404 square-feet of new construction. This scope includes an addition to the existing Self Realization Fellowship International Headquarters building, a new garden and maintenance workshop consisting of two connected wings, garden shrine, mechanical central plant, fire pump room, and a pedestrian bridge/walkway within an existing garden. The project also includes an entry kiosk and the reconstruction of the historic Cable Car Building with a basement addition, and remodel of the existing visitor center, following the demolition of approximately 3,773 square-feet of existing floor area, on a 543,278.2-square-foot lot that is within the Mount Washington-Glassell Park Specific Plan area. The project would result in a net addition of 12,631 square-feet and a total of 44,853 square-feet. Although the site comprises approximately 12.47 acres of lot area, the project scope is limited to a portion of the site that is approximately 3.5 acres. As a project located on a portion of a site that is less than or equal to five (5) acres, the proposed scope of work is eligible for a Class 32 Categorical Exemption. Additionally, the project site has been identified as a historic resource by the City of Los Angeles and is improved with designated Historic Cultural Monument No. 845 (Self-Realization Fellowship International Headquarters / Mount Washington Hotel). Per an email from Office of Historic Resources (OHR) staff dated October 11, 2024, a Secretary of the Interior’s Standards Compliance Report was prepared for the project by Jenna Snow, Historic Preservation Consulting, in August 2024. The Report was reviewed by OHR and staff confirmed in this email that the report is acceptable. As a project involving the rehabilitation, maintenance, and reconstruction of a historical resource consistent with the Secretary of Interior’s Standards, the proposed scope of work is eligible for a Class 31 Categorical Exemption. Approximately 10,361 cubic yards of total grading is proposed in conjunction with an application for a haul route for the export of approximately 7,505 cubic yards of earth. The proposed grading for cut is 8,933 cubic yards and the proposed grading for fill is 1,428 cubic yards. A project requires a haul route when a site is located in the Hillside Area or a Special Bureau of Engineering (BOE) Grading Area and involves the import or export of earth material of 1,000 cubic yards or more. The subject site is located within the Hillside Area and a Special Bureau of Engineering (BOE) Grading Area and proposes the export of approximately 7,505 cubic yards of earth. Therefore, a haul route is required. Additionally, the project proposes a total of 34 retaining walls, 12 of which are new walls, 14 of which are full or partial replacements of existing walls (some of which are block walls), five (5) of which are decorative garden walls, and three (3) of which are small walls to protect trees on the property. The proposed retaining walls range from 15 feet to 210 feet in length and range from 0.5 feet to 9.9 feet in maximum height above finished grade. The Applicant retained an arborist to perform a survey of trees on and adjacent to the project site. Per the Arborist Report that was prepared by Christy Cuba, ASCA Registered Consulting Arborist #502; Cy Carlberg, ASCA Registered Consulting Arborist #405; Scott McAllaster, ISA Certified Arborist #WE7011A; and Daniel Cowell, Staff Arborist; dated March 4, 2026, there are 45 street trees in the adjacent public right-of-way, 93 Protected Trees on-site, and 1,164 non-protected trees on-site. There are also 20 off-site private property trees. 10 Protected Trees (four (4) Southern California Black Walnuts, one (1) Coast Live Oak, two (2) Mexican Elderberry shrubs, and three (3) Toyon shrubs) are proposed for removal and 40 Protected Trees (16 Southern California Black Walnuts, four (4) Coast Live Oaks, eight (8) Mexican Elderberry shrubs, and 12 Toyon shrubs) are proposed for replacement on the subject lot. The Arborist Report was reviewed, and the Urban Forestry Division Referral Form was signed by Urban Forestry Division staff on March 20, 2026. Additionally, Urban Forestry Division staff stamped a Tree Replacement plan on April 9, 2026. This environmental analysis does not authorize the removal of any street trees without the prior approval of Urban Forestry, in compliance with LAMC Section 62.9169 and 62.170 and their applicable findings.
records.lastNote: The proposed project includes the rehabilitation, expansion, and construction, use, and maintenance of historic church-related facilities measuring approximately 16,404 square-feet of new construction.

records.addr: S&W Atlas Iron and Metal Company Interim Soil Vapor Extraction Workplan
records.originalTitle: S&W Atlas Iron and Metal Company Interim Soil Vapor Extraction Workplan
records.desc: Project Description: The Interim Soil Vapor Extraction Workplan commits the S&W Atlas Iron and Metal Company (Facility) to install and operate an Soil Vapor Extraction (SVE) system to address volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in soil gas at the south and southwest areas of the Facility located at 10019 South Alameda Street in Los Angeles. The project activities include installing one SVE pilot well, four additional SVE wells connected to a vacuum extraction unit, and treating the extracted vapors before discharge. The SVE system will protect adjacent properties and buildings while the full site investigation continues. Background: The 3.28-acre Facility is located in an area that was historically used for industrial, commercial, school, and residential development. The Facility is currently covered by impervious surfaces consisting of asphalt, concrete, and one existing warehouse. A second warehouse that previously existed in the west-central portion of the Facility was demolished in September 2022. The Facility was formerly used by Atlas for scrap metal recycling operations, which ceased in 2025. As of January 19, 2026, equipment remaining onsite includes excavators, material handlers, shearing equipment, shipping containers, one roll-off bin for retired items, and one roll-off bin for trash. Prior to ceasing operations, DTSC conditionally approved of the Scrap Removal Work Plan on July 1, 2025. Metal scrap removal began on July 8, 2025, and was completed on August 22, 2025. Air monitoring is ongoing at the Facility in accordance with the Revised Phase I Air Monitoring Workplan dated February 1, 2023. On March 10, 2021, the California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) issued an Enforcement Order for Corrective Action, Docket No. HWCA-FY20/21-008 (Order), which established several required actions to evaluate if the Facility released chromium, copper, lead, nickel, zinc, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), used oil, and/or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) to the subsurface. Previous Investigations: A Facility Investigation (FI) and a Supplemental Site Investigation (SSI) were conducted from 2023 to 2025 to assess Areas of Concern (AOCs) and subsurface impacts. Investigations identified releases of VOCs, metals, total petroleum hydrocarbons, and polychlorinated biphenyls in soil and soil gas. Based on the FI and SSI, the AOCs identified by DTSC are as follows: 1- Receiving Area, 2- Roll-Off Bins, 3- Metal Scrap Piles, 4- Warehouse No.1, 5- Container Loader Area, 6- Clarifier and Associated Piping System, 7- Gated Area, 8- Broken Cement Areas and 9- Lead-Impacted Soil North of the Former Warehouse No. 2. Following the review of the Facility Investigation Sampling Results dated December 12, 2025, DTSC requested that Atlas implement an interim measure to address VOCs in the southwest corner of the Facility while the full investigation of the facility is completed. Project Activities: The project activities consist of installing a skid-mounted SVE system with a vapor/liquid separator, an extraction blower with a maximum flow rate of 300 standard cubic feet per minute (SCFM), and an air-to-air heat exchanger. The SVE equipment will be connected to two vessels with granular activated carbon and one vessel with granular activated carbon and an inorganic oxidizing agent in series. The SVE blower inlet will be connected to the new SVE wells using polyvinyl chloride (PVC) piping and high-pressure vacuum hose. Five existing soil vapor probes (SVPs), SG-10, SG-14, SG-16, SG-17, and SG-18will be used for pilot testing. A chain link security fence will be installed around the SVE skid and carbon vessels. Publicly visible signage with a 24-hour emergency contact telephone number will be displayed on the system fencing. The South Coast Air Quality Metropolitan District (SCAQMD) Rule 1166 and Rule 203 will require notification of the SVE operation for sensitive receptors located less than a quarter mile away including residences, schools, or childcare. The pilot test will be conducted in 5 days or less. The pilot test results will be evaluated to estimate an ROI, which will be used as the basis for the number of wells and spacing between the wells in the interim measure. Although not anticipated, in the event biological, cultural or historical resources are discovered in the course of project activities, work will be suspended while a qualified biologist, cultural or historical specialist makes an assessment of the area and arrangements are made to protect or preserve any resources that are discovered. If human remains are discovered, no further disturbance will occur in the location where the remains are found, and the County Coroner will be notified pursuant to the Health and Safety Code, Chapter 2, Section 7050.5.

records.addr: 14430 Vanowen Street, Land Acquisition, Permanent Affordable Housing; Land Bank Pilot Program Site #3
records.originalTitle: 14430 Vanowen Street, Land Acquisition, Permanent Affordable Housing; Land Bank Pilot Program Site #3
records.desc: On July 7, 2026, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors (Board), approved and authorized the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), or her designee, to execute a Purchase Sale Agreement (PSA) for the 20,328-square-foot (per survey) property located at 14430 W. Vanowen Street in the Van Nuys neighborhood of the Van-Nuys-North Sherman Oaks Community Planning area in the City of Los Angeles and to establish and approve an affordable housing project as discussed below. The purchase is part of the CEO-HI (CEO-Homeless Initiative, now known as the County’s Department of Homeless Services and Housing) Land Bank Pilot Program. The Board established the Pilot Program on June 14, 2022, to create new opportunities for affordable housing in areas experiencing and set to experience rapid gentrification and displacement. The project would include an approximately seven to eight-story (approximately 78-feet-tall) mixed-use affordable housing development with up to 195 units and up to 6.5: 1 Floor Area Ratio; parking would be provided according to code; the project could also include 1,500 square feet of community-serving commercial space and an approximately 3,000-square-foot community room and/or amenity space primarily to serve project residents. The property would include minor landscaping and low-level security lighting. The site currently contains an asphalt parking lot that has been used by adjacent uses but is currently unused. There is one ornamental street tree in the sidewalk in front of the site and an ornamental palm tree in the alley to the east of the site that abuts the site that could be impacted by the project. Subsurface parking is not anticipated. The proposed building foundation design and construction method have not been identified but could include localized foundation piles extending to some depth but more likely spread footings or mat slab foundation extending up to 10 feet to 20 feet below grade. However, the quantity of earth that would be disturbed is anticipated to be relatively minor. Construction is anticipated to take about 24 months. The project would include sustainability features. The site is identified as a Lower Income Rezoning Housing Element site in the City of Los Angeles Housing Element and with more than 20% of the units to be affordable to lower income households the development of housing would be a by-right project in the City of Los Angeles (Government Code Section 65583.2(i)). records.addr: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California
records.originalTitle: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, California
records.desc: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20, Sec. 66270.61, has issued an Emergency Permit to University of California, Los Angeles, (EPA ID# CAD042231431) to treat hazardous waste through a controlled reaction with chemical solutions. Specifically, three (3) 1-liter containers of Isoamyl Alcohol, one (1) 50-gram container of 1-Hydroxybenzotriazole, and one (1) 500-gram container of Picric Acid must be stabilized prior to transport to an authorized hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facility. These chemicals are currently being stored at the University of California, Los Angeles located at 550 Charles E. Young Drive West, Los Angeles, California 90095. DTSC has determined as a safety precaution to prevent an accident or severe injury, an Emergency Permit should be issued for Clean Harbors Environmental Services (Clean Harbors) to chemically stabilize the hazardous waste prior to storage and eventual transportation off-site. Background: The container has peroxide formation present on either the inside, outside, or the bottom of the chemical's containers, as well as the thread container caps. The presence of peroxide formation may be unstable at relatively low concentrations, resulting in fire and/or explosion if improperly handled. Also shock-sensitive materials can decompose or detonate with external energy when dry or concentrated. If the material is improperly handled, there is a potential for a reaction, which includes fire, deflagration, or detonation. Due to the presence of peroxide forming and shock sensitive materials, DTSC considers these chemicals to be an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment. Chemical stabilization is recommended prior to transport to a permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facility. Project Activities: The treatment of these hazardous wastes involves the addition of a solution to the containers in a controlled manner to reduce the reactive or ignitable characteristics of the chemicals. Treatment will take place within a designated exclusion zone. Only technicians from Clean Harbors will be allowed in the exclusion zone. Movement, preparation, and treatment of the container will be in accordance with established standards. Within 10 business days of the expiration of this permit, the University of California, Los Angeles will submit a final report, signed in accordance with Title 22, CCR Sec. 66270.11(d). The report shall include certification that the treatment area has been cleared of all residual hazardous waste generated from this emergency treatment and all generated waste has been properly managed. The Emergency Permit is effective beginning July 31, 2026 and shall expire on September 29, 2026.

records.addr: Adopt Emergency Regulations to Amend Title 22, California Code of Regulations, Division 4.5, Chapter 11, Appendix X, Subsection (c) and Chapter 10, Subsection 6
records.originalTitle: Adopt Emergency Regulations to Amend Title 22, California Code of Regulations, Division 4.5, Chapter 11, Appendix X, Subsection (c) and Chapter 10, Subsection 6
records.desc: The Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) proposes to approve an emergency rulemaking amendment to add to the existing list of Covered Electronic Devices (CED’s) within the California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 11, Appendix X, Subsection (c) and Chapter 10, Subsection 66260.201(e). This emergency rulemaking will amend the list of CED’s to include the new devices and provide clarity to impacted entities. The amended regulations will safeguard California’s environment against potential hazardous constituents found in discarded electronic devices and expand financial incentives for proper end-of-life management which will lead to an increase in the amount of CED’s recycled and decrease the amount of hazardous electronic waste illegally disposed of in landfills. Background: California enacted the Electronic Waste Recycling Act (Act) of 2003 through Senate Bill 20, which was amended through Senate Bill 50 in 2005 to incentivize collectors and recyclers to provide ample opportunities to California residents for recycling, thereby discouraging the illegal disposal of hazardous electronic waste in landfills and establish a funding system for the collection and recycling of certain electronic waste identified as the Covered Electronic Waste Recycling Program (Program). A CED is a video display device containing a screen greater than four inches, measured diagonally, that is found to exhibit the hazardous waste characteristic of toxicity when discarded. The Program requires consumers to pay a fee on all CED’s at the time of retail purchase. Retailers can also elect to pay the fee on behalf of consumers. The retailers remit the fees they collect to the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA). CDTFA deposits the fees into a designated account used to provide payments to approved collectors and recyclers for the recovery, processing, and recycling of CED’s. The Act tasks the California Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery (CalRecycle) with administering the payment system for collectors and recyclers. The Act also tasks DTSC with (a) developing regulations for the proper management of discarded CED’s, (b) identifying in regulations any devices that exhibit, or are presumed to exhibit, the hazardous waste characteristic of toxicity as a CED, and (c) conducting inspections and compliance activities. Under Health and Safety Code section 25214.10.1 subsection (c), DTSC has the authority to presume that devices are hazardous waste when discarded. Thus, based on DTSC’s presumption authority and the analytical testing data of components commonly used in the manufacture of video display devices as described below, DTSC has identified that these devices are CED’s and are hazardous waste when discarded. In 2021, DTSC’s Environmental Chemistry Lab conducted analytical testing on six different device categories that met the definition of a CED under Public Resources Code section 42463. Specifically, DTSC tested the printed circuit boards and screen materials from these devices. Analytical testing results concluded that these devices exhibit the hazardous waste characteristic of toxicity identified in Article 4 of chapter 11 and exceed the California hazardous waste total threshold concentrations described in section 66261.24(a)(2)(A) for copper, lead, and nickel. Therefore, these devices are deemed hazardous wastes when discarded and were added to the list of CED’s in emergency regulations, OAL reference# R-021-09E (readopted in 2023 and 2025). Project Activities: The proposed rulemaking will add five new device categories to the list of CED’s found in Chapter 11, Appendix X, Subsection (c) and Chapter 10, Subsection 66260.201(e). The new device categories consist of the following: • Portable gaming devices with an integrated screen; • Home surveillance monitors with an integrated or dedicated screen; • Smart mirrors and any other mirrors capable of displaying video; • Digital picture frames capable of displaying video; and • Smart remote controllers with an integrated screen capable of displaying video.
